description: Understand opening, closing, and self-closing tags.
definition: Tags describe the role of content on a web page.
rule: Most elements have an opening tag, content, and a closing tag.
tip: A slash marks the closing tag.
caution: Void elements, like images, have no closing tag in HTML.
exercise: Write a paragraph element containing your name.

description: Learn the difference between <h1> and <h6>.
definition: Headings organize a page into meaningful sections.
rule: H one is the highest heading level; H six is the lowest.
tip: Use heading levels to describe the hierarchy of your content.
caution: Choose headings for meaning, rather than just their default size.
exercise: Create a page title and a heading for its first section.

description:
Add readable text to a webpage with

.
definition: A paragraph element groups a piece of text into a paragraph.
rule: Wrap each paragraph in opening and closing P tags.
tip: Browsers normally leave space between paragraphs.
caution: Extra spaces and line breaks in source code usually collapse.
exercise: Write two paragraphs about something you enjoy.

topic: How to Add Links in HTML
description: Create clickable links using <a href>.
definition: Links connect your page to other pages or resources.
rule: The anchor element creates the link; H ref supplies its destination.
tip: The text between the tags becomes the clickable label.
caution: Use descriptive link text so people know where they are going.
exercise: Add a link to a website you find useful.

topic: How to Add Images in HTML
description: Display images using and understand alt.
definition: An image element embeds a picture in your page.
rule: Source identifies the image file; alt provides a text alternative.
tip: Describe useful image content in the alternative text.
caution: The image element is void, so it has no closing tag.
exercise: Add a local image with a useful text description.

description: Create ordered and unordered lists.
definition: Lists group related items in a meaningful order.
rule: Use an unordered list for bullets, and an ordered list for numbering.
tip: Each list item belongs inside an L I element.
caution: Pick numbering when the sequence of the items matters.
exercise: Create a numbered list of three steps in your morning routine.

description: Add buttons and understand their basic purpose.
definition: A button is a control that people can activate.
rule: Use the button element to create an accessible native control.
tip: JavaScript can listen for a click and perform an action.
caution: Inside a form, specify the type to avoid accidental submission.
exercise: Create a button with a clear action label.

description: Learn how id, class, and other attributes work.
definition: Attributes provide additional information about an element.
rule: Write attributes inside the opening tag, commonly as name and value.
tip: An I D identifies one element; a class can group several.
caution: Keep each I D unique within the document.
exercise: Give two paragraphs the same class and different identifiers.

description: Understand block and inline containers.
definition: Div and span are generic containers for grouping content.
rule: A div is block level by default; a span is inline.
tip: Use a span to group words within a line of text.
caution: Prefer a meaningful semantic element when one fits your content.
exercise: Wrap a sentence in a div and one word in a span.

description: Add notes to code without displaying them.
definition: HTML comments are notes that browsers do not display as page content.
rule: A comment begins with an angle bracket, exclamation mark, and two hyphens.
tip: It ends with two hyphens and a closing angle bracket.
caution: Comments remain visible in source code, so never put secrets there.
exercise: Add a short comment explaining the next section of your page.

description:
Use
and
appropriately.
definition: Line breaks and thematic breaks have different meanings.
rule: B R creates a line break; H R marks a thematic break.
tip: A line break suits addresses and lines of a poem.
caution: Use C S S spacing instead of repeated break elements for layout.
exercise: Write a two-line address, then add a thematic break below it.

description: Organize information using rows and columns.
definition: Tables organize data into rows and columns.
rule: T R defines a row, T H a header, and T D a cell.
tip: A caption can describe what the table contains.
caution: Use tables for data, rather than for arranging an entire page.
exercise: Create a table showing two skills and their practice time.

description: Build your first form with <form>.
definition: A form groups controls that collect information from a user.
rule: Give controls labels so people can understand what to enter.
tip: The name attribute identifies a field when form data is submitted.
caution: A form alone does not save data; it needs a submission handler.
exercise: Create a labeled email field and a submit button.

description: Explore text, email, password, and number inputs.
definition: Input types tell a browser what kind of value to collect.
rule: Email, password, and number types offer different input behavior.
tip: An email field can participate in browser validation.
caution: Masking a password field does not encrypt or securely store its value.
exercise: Try three input types and compare their behavior.

description: Let users select one or multiple options.
definition: Checkboxes allow independent choices; radio buttons select within a group.
preview:
HTML

CSS

Beginner
rule: Use the same name for radio buttons that belong to one group.
tip: Checkboxes are useful when several options may be selected together.
caution: Associate every control with a label, including checkboxes and radios.
exercise: Create two skill checkboxes and a radio group for experience level.

description: Create dropdown selections using <select>.
definition: A select element presents a list of choices.
rule: Each option inside the select becomes one available choice.
tip: A value attribute can specify the data submitted for an option.
caution: Use a label so the purpose of the selection is clear.
exercise: Create a dropdown with three learning goals.

description: Understand header, nav, main, and footer.
definition: Semantic HTML describes the purpose of your content.
rule: Header, navigation, main, and footer give sections meaningful roles.
tip: These landmarks help assistive technology users navigate a page.
caution: Choose elements by meaning, rather than their appearance.
exercise: Replace generic page containers with suitable semantic elements.

description: Embed audio and video on your website.
definition: HTML can embed sound and video with native playback controls.
code:
<video controls
       src="lesson.mp4">
 Your browser needs video support.
</video>
rule: Use audio for sound and video for moving pictures.
tip: The controls attribute adds the browser playback interface.
caution: Add captions for spoken video content, and avoid relying on autoplay.
exercise: Embed a local video and show its playback controls.

description: Understand page titles, descriptions, and viewport settings.
definition: Document metadata describes a page to browsers and other services.
rule: The title element supplies the browser tab title.
tip: The viewport meta tag supports appropriate sizing on mobile screens.
caution: Metadata belongs in the head; visible page content belongs in the body.
exercise: Add a useful title and a viewport declaration to your document.

description: Discover how CSS makes webpages beautiful.
definition: C S S controls how your HTML content looks.
rule: A rule combines a selector with declarations inside braces.
tip: Each declaration pairs a property with a value.
caution: Keep the content meaningful even before its styling loads.
exercise: Change a paragraph color and font size.

description: Compare inline, internal, and external CSS.
definition: You can add C S S inline, inside a document, or in a separate file.
code:
<!-- In the document head -->
<link rel="stylesheet"
      href="styles.css">
rule: Inline styles use an attribute; internal styles use a style element.
tip: An external stylesheet can be shared across several pages.
caution: Keep larger projects organized with a separate stylesheet.
exercise: Create a styles file and connect it to your HTML document.

description: Use HEX, RGB, and named colors.
definition: C S S colors can be written as names, hexadecimal values, or color functions.
rule: Different color formats can describe the same visible color.
tip: Choose text and background colors that remain easy to read.
caution: Color alone should not be the only way to communicate meaning.
exercise: Style a heading, paragraph, and link using three color formats.

description: Change font size, weight, spacing, and alignment.
definition: Text properties control the presentation of written content.
preview:
HELLO

Readable text starts with good spacing.
rule: Font size, weight, and line height affect readability.
tip: Relative units can help text scale with user preferences.
caution: Use real heading elements for structure, even when styling changes their size.
exercise: Give a heading bold weight and a paragraph comfortable line spacing.

description: Add colors, gradients, and background images.
definition: Background properties paint the area behind an element.
rule: Start with a solid color, or combine colors in a gradient.
tip: A background image can be sized and positioned separately.
caution: Keep foreground text readable across the entire background.
exercise: Give a card a two-color gradient background.

description: Understand margin, padding, border, and content.
definition: The box model describes the space occupied by an element.
rule: From inside out, it has content, padding, border, and margin.
tip: Padding is inside the border; margin is outside it.
caution: With border box sizing, declared width includes padding and borders.
exercise: Give a card padding, a border, and outside margin.

phase: Phase 3 — Build Beautiful Websites with CSS
description: Understand how to target HTML elements.
definition: Classes and identifiers let C S S select particular elements.
rule: A dot selects a class; a hash selects an identifier.
tip: Reuse a class to apply the same style to several elements.
caution: Keep identifiers unique, and avoid unnecessary selector specificity.
exercise: Style two elements with one shared class.

phase: Phase 3 — Build Beautiful Websites with CSS
description: Learn block, inline, and inline-block.
definition: Display controls how an element participates in layout.
rule: Block elements normally start a new line; inline elements flow with text.
tip: Inline block boxes flow inline while accepting width and height.
caution: Display none removes an element from layout and the accessibility tree.
exercise: Compare a block container with two inline block labels.

phase: Phase 3 — Build Beautiful Websites with CSS
description: Align elements horizontally and vertically.
definition: Flexbox arranges items along one main axis.
rule: Turn the parent into a flex container to arrange its children.
tip: Justify content controls the main axis; align items controls the cross axis.
caution: Those axes change when the flex direction changes.
exercise: Center three items in a row with an even gap.

phase: Phase 3 — Build Beautiful Websites with CSS
description: Build clean layouts with rows and columns.
definition: Grid arranges items in rows and columns.
rule: Define columns on the parent and place items inside it.
tip: A fractional unit shares available space between grid tracks.
caution: Use grid for layouts that need coordinated rows and columns.
exercise: Create a two-column gallery with four cards.

phase: Phase 3 — Build Beautiful Websites with CSS
description: Understand relative, absolute, fixed, and sticky.
definition: Position changes how an element is placed in a layout.
rule: Relative positioning can establish a containing block for an absolute child.
tip: Fixed positioning usually anchors to the viewport; sticky follows a scroll threshold.
caution: Absolute elements leave normal flow, so reserve space when needed.
exercise: Place a small badge in the corner of a card.

phase: Phase 3 — Build Beautiful Websites with CSS
description: Make buttons react when users hover.
definition: The hover selector styles an element while a pointer rests over it.
rule: Combine a hover rule with a transition for a smooth change.
tip: Focus visible can provide a matching cue for keyboard users.
caution: Hover is not reliable on touchscreens; keep essential actions accessible.
exercise: Add hover and keyboard focus styles to one button.

phase: Phase 3 — Build Beautiful Websites with CSS
description: Create attractive cards and buttons.
definition: Borders define edges, while shadows can suggest depth.
rule: A border has a width, style, and color.
tip: Border radius rounds the corners; box shadow paints a shadow.
caution: Keep shadows subtle enough that text and boundaries remain clear.
exercise: Create a rounded card with a border and soft shadow.

phase: Phase 3 — Build Beautiful Websites with CSS
description: Make websites work on mobile and desktop.
definition: Responsive design adapts a page to different screen sizes.
rule: Use flexible layouts so content can rearrange as space changes.
tip: Responsive images and a viewport declaration support mobile layouts.
caution: Test real content at narrow widths instead of targeting only one device.
exercise: Make a card layout that works on a phone and desktop.

phase: Phase 3 — Build Beautiful Websites with CSS
description: Change layouts based on screen size.
definition: Media queries apply styles when specified conditions match.
rule: A minimum width query can add a wider layout when space is available.
tip: Write the narrow layout first, then add larger-screen adjustments.
caution: Choose breakpoints where the content needs them, rather than by device names.
exercise: Stack two cards on mobile and place them together on wider screens.

phase: Phase 3 — Build Beautiful Websites with CSS
description: Create movement using transitions and keyframes.
definition: Transitions and keyframes create changes over time.
rule: A transition responds to a changed property; keyframes define an animation sequence.
tip: Opacity and transform are useful properties for simple interface motion.
caution: Respect reduced motion preferences and avoid unnecessary movement.
exercise: Animate a card entrance with a short fade and upward movement.

description: Learn how JavaScript adds website interactivity.
definition: JavaScript adds logic and interactive behavior to web pages.
rule: A script can respond when a user activates a button.
tip: Use JavaScript to update content, validate input, or manage application state.
caution: Keep HTML structure and accessible controls in place before adding behavior.
exercise: Make a button respond with a greeting.

description: Understand let, const, and storing values.
definition: Variables give names to values used by your program.
rule: Use let when you need to reassign a variable.
tip: Use const when the binding should not be reassigned.
caution: Const does not make the contents of an object immutable.
exercise: Store your name and a score, then increase the score.

description: Explore strings, numbers, booleans, and more.
definition: JavaScript values have different types with different behavior.
rule: Text is a string, a numeric value is a number, and true is a boolean.
tip: The type of operator can help inspect the type of a value.
caution: A number inside quotation marks is a string, which changes some operations.
exercise: Create a string, a number, and a boolean.

description: Perform basic calculations and comparisons.
definition: Operators perform actions such as arithmetic and comparisons.
rule: Plus can add numbers, and comparison operators return boolean results.
tip: Strict equality compares values without converting their types.
caution: Plus can also join strings, so check the types of your inputs.
exercise: Calculate a total and compare it with a target value.

description: Create reusable blocks of code.
definition: A function groups instructions into a reusable operation.
rule: Parameters receive input, and return sends a result back to the caller.
tip: Call the function with an argument to run its instructions.
caution: Returning a value and displaying a value are different actions.
exercise: Write a function that returns the sum of two numbers.

description: Make decisions based on conditions.
definition: If and else let a program choose between actions.
rule: The if branch runs when its condition is truthy.
tip: The else branch handles the alternative when that condition is false.
caution: Use comparison operators in conditions, rather than accidental assignment.
exercise: Display a different message depending on a practice score.

description: Repeat tasks using for and while.
definition: Loops repeat instructions without writing the same code repeatedly.
rule: A for loop can initialize a counter, check a condition, and update it.
tip: Each pass through the loop is called an iteration.
caution: Make sure the condition can become false to avoid an infinite loop.
exercise: Print the numbers from one through five with a loop.

description: Store and access multiple values.
definition: An array stores an ordered collection of values.
rule: Array positions start at zero, so index zero gives the first item.
tip: Push appends an item, and length reports the number of items.
caution: An array with three items has a last index of two.
exercise: Create an array of three skills and read its first item.

description: Organize related information with properties.
definition: Objects organize information as named properties and their values.
rule: Use a property name to access one piece of an object.
tip: Dot notation works with ordinary identifier-style property names.
caution: Use bracket notation when a property name comes from a variable.
exercise: Create an object describing a learner and read its name.

description: Change HTML content with JavaScript.
definition: The document object model represents a page as objects JavaScript can change.
rule: Select an element, then change its text content.
tip: Event listeners can trigger these updates when a user takes an action.
caution: Ensure the element exists before using it, and prefer text content for plain text.
exercise: Change a heading when someone presses a button.

description: Combine HTML and CSS into a simple profile design.
definition: A profile card combines meaningful content with a small reusable layout.
rule: Start with an article, a heading, and a short introduction.
tip: Add padding, a border, and consistent spacing in your stylesheet.
caution: If you include a portrait, give it appropriate alternative text.
exercise: Build a card with your name, a short bio, and one useful link.

description: Create a menu that adapts to mobile screens.
definition: A responsive navigation bar keeps important links usable at different widths.
rule: Put navigation links inside a navigation element.
tip: Flex wrapping lets links move to another line when space is tight.
caution: A collapsible menu needs keyboard support and an accessible toggle button.
exercise: Build three navigation links that wrap on a narrow screen.

description: Make interactive plus, minus, and reset buttons.
definition: A counter connects application state to visible output.
rule: Store the count in a variable, and update it when a button is pressed.
tip: After every change, update the text shown on the page.
caution: Select the button and output elements before attaching event listeners.
exercise: Build plus, minus, and reset controls for your counter.

description: Add and remove tasks using JavaScript.
definition: A to-do list turns user input into items that can be managed.
rule: Create a list item, assign its text, then append it to the list.
tip: Add a remove control for each task and clear the input after adding.
caution: Reject empty input, and use text content when displaying user-entered text.
exercise: Build an add button, a task list, and a remove action.

topic: Publish Your First Website for Free
description: Deploy a static website using GitHub Pages.
definition: GitHub Pages can publish a static website from a repository.
preview:
✓ Your site is live

Hello, web!
rule: Add your static files to a repository and configure Pages in its settings.
tip: For a simple branch deployment, select the source branch and folder.
caution: Pages serves static files; it does not run a custom application server.
exercise: Publish a small site, then open its Pages address on your phone.
